coimbras.name: Coimbras Chapel and House
coimbras.short: A 16th-century tower chapel with a carved stone altarpiece and tiles of the Creation
coimbras.long: João de Coimbra, vicar-general of the Archdiocese of Braga, built this tower-like chapel in 1525–1528. Outside it has battlements, statues and a porch closed by a wrought-iron grille. Inside are a ribbed vault, a painted stone altarpiece and blue-and-white tiles. The neighbouring Coimbras House keeps its Manueline windows: it was taken down in the early 20th century and rebuilt beside the chapel in 1924.
coimbras.history:
The founder was Dr João de Coimbra, vicar-general of the archdiocese under Archbishop Diogo de Sousa. In 1505 he bought a house beside the church of São João do Souto, and in 1525 he began a private chapel next to it, dedicated to the Immaculate Conception. A Latin inscription on the wall records that he consecrated it to the Mother of God in 1528. In 1530 he founded an entailed estate: his lands and houses passed to the eldest sons of the family, and the chapel became the family burial place.

The chapel looks like a square, battlemented tower. Masons from Biscay built it, and the sculptor Hodart carved the statues outside. In front of the door stands a columned porch with a wrought-iron grille and the Coimbra arms; above the portal are the arms of Archbishop Diogo de Sousa.

Inside, gilded rosettes stud the ribbed vault, with the founder’s arms at the centre. The Renaissance stone altarpiece is attributed to the young João de Ruão. Its niches hold painted figures of the Virgin and Child, Saint Anne and Saint Joachim. Nearby is a sculpted Entombment of Christ, which gave the chapel its other name, Senhor Morto, “the Dead Lord”. Blue-and-white 18th-century tiles with scenes of the Creation cover the walls.

The chapel once adjoined the Romanesque church of São João do Souto. The church was later rebuilt, but the chapel stayed as it was, and in 1910 it became a National Monument. The Coimbras House stood about a hundred metres away. In the early 20th century the city cleared the square and the house was dismantled. In 1924 it was rebuilt beside the chapel, keeping its Manueline windows and doors. The founder’s descendants still gather here for Mass on 8 December, as João de Coimbra wished.
facts: A Latin inscription on the wall dates the chapel’s consecration to 1528.
The stone altarpiece is attributed to the young João de Ruão.
The chapel has been a National Monument since 16 June 1910.
The house was dismantled in the early 20th century and rebuilt in 1924.
The founder’s descendants gather here every year for Mass on 8 December.
coimbras.tip: The chapel stands on Largo de São João do Souto, three minutes’ walk from the cathedral. Entry is paid; check opening hours on the Visit Braga website. Look closely at the porch grille: cherubs hold up the Coimbra arms. São Marcos Church is a couple of minutes away on foot.
